extracted.intended_audience: regulatory attorneys, agency rulewriters, policy analysts, and stakeholders participating in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: A Federal Register search-results listing of agency rules, proposed rules, and notices that cite Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and discuss its effects on statutory interpretation, rulemaking authority, rescissions, and APA compliance. Useful for practitioners assessing how to draft, defend, or challenge regulations post‑Loper Bright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-best-reading requirement for statutory interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, agencies must ensure that a regulation "matches the single, best meaning of the statute"; courts will determine the best interpretation rather than deferring to an agency's permissible interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated across entries: agencies are instructed to review regulations and return them to the language that "better implements the best reading" of the statute; Executive Orders direct rescission of regulations "based on anything other than the best reading of the underlying statutory authority." Example uses: rescinding ESA "harm" definition, revising PECE reliance, rescinding SMCRA and other rules that exceed statutory authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independent-judgment standard (no Chevron deference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must exercise independent judgment in statutory interpretation; federal agency interpretations receive no special judicial deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrased in multiple excerpts as: "the reviewing court itself must determine the best interpretation of a statute," and courts will "apply all relevant interpretive tools" to conclude the best reading. Agencies should anticipate courts reexamining past decisions and not relying on Chevron as a backstop (e.g., circuit opinions that cited Chevron may be subject to reexamination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authorization as the controlling question
rubrics_metrics.description: The dispositive inquiry is whether the statute authorizes the challenged agency action; agency action must be within what the statute permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted formulation: under Loper Bright, “the question that matters” is whether “the statute authorizes the challenged agency action.” Agencies should test regulations against the statute’s text and purpose and rescind or revise those lacking clear statutory authorization (cited across EPA, DOI, DOL, DOE entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to Administrative Procedure Act (APA) standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency actions must not be arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law; procedural requirements (e.g., notice-and-comment) must be followed where APA demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents cite APA judicial-review standards when evaluating proposed rescissions or revisions (e.g., DOE, NCUA, MSHA). Example anti-pattern: skipping notice-and-comment for substantive changes (MSHA roof-control plan additional-measures sentence criticized for skipping notice and comment). Agencies must provide reasoned explanations and follow required procedures when altering rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescind or revise regulations not based on the best reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Branch directives and multiple agency proposals state agencies should rescind or revise regulations that are 'based on anything other than the best reading of the underlying statutory authority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are actively proposing rescissions (e.g., SMCRA 10-day notices rule, EPA and DOI regulatory revisions) and cite E.O.s and Loper Bright as grounds. Guidance here is operational: review existing regulations, identify provisions lacking textual/statutory support, propose rescission or return-to-prior-language where the prior language better implements the 'best reading.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory definitions must reflect the statute's single best meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining statutory terms in regulation (e.g., ESA's definition of 'harm'), the regulatory definition must align with the single best meaning of the statutory term rather than broader administrative constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proposal to rescind the regulatory definition of 'harm' because it 'runs contrary to the best meaning of the statutory term "take."' Agencies should reexamine definitional language and change definitions that cannot be justified as the best reading of the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on agency-interpretation-based policies that lack clear statutory grounding (PECE/other policies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that rest principally on agency interpretation rather than the best reading of the statute are vulnerable post-Loper Bright and should be justified or revised to show textual statutory support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Fish and Wildlife Service PECE example: commenters argued PECE "relies on agency interpretation rather than the 'best reading' of the ESA," making it legally indefensible under current precedent. Agencies should document textual bases for interpretive policies or revise/eliminate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: When changing substantive program criteria or protections, prefer targeted, text‑based rulemaking (e.g., species-specific rules vs 'blanket' rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where statute allows discretion in creating protective measures, agencies are moving toward crafting targeted, textually justified rules (for example, replacing ESA 'blanket rule' protections with species-specific 4(d) rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FWS proposes removing the 'blanket rule' option to create species‑specific rules—guidance implies agencies should tailor rules and articulate statutory bases for distinctions rather than relying on broad, catch‑all regulatory devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamine reliance on prior precedent that invoked Chevron deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency reliance on judicial precedents that accepted agency interpretations under Chevron may be undermined; those precedents may be subject to reexamination under the new independent-judgment standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple excerpts note commenters arguing that circuit opinions "relied on Chevron deference" and thus may be invalid in light of Loper Bright; agencies and litigants should be prepared to address whether prior case law remains persuasive absent Chevron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and solicit public input when altering compliance dates, standards, or significant regulatory provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies propose to amend compliance dates or significant standards, they should solicit comments and data to support any change and to demonstrate statutory authority for the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE notice of petition for rulemaking and other agency proposals explicitly seek comment on whether to grant petitions or amend compliance dates; this illustrates the expectation that substantive regulatory changes be justified with record evidence and public participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational practices and investigatory procedures must conform to statutory text and agency-authority limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency investigatory or enforcement practices (e.g., OSMRE coordination with States; MSHA District Manager authority to add plan measures) must be consistent with the best reading of the enabling statute and not expand agency power beyond statutory grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSMRE and MSHA examples show agencies proposing to return to prior language or remove provisions that could be read to exceed statutory authority, reflecting a rubric that administrative procedures and delegated discretion be tightly tied to textual authorization.
